Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer):
That, in relation to Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of the second reading stage of the said Bill; and
That 15 minutes before the expiry of the time provided for the consideration of government business on the above-mentioned sitting day, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted, if necessary, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary to dispose of the said stage of the said Bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the time has come to have a vote on Bill C-70, and that is why this motion is before the House. For many years Members of Parliament have argued that when a Budget is introduced in the House of Commons and is passed after six days of full debate, the Bills which flow from it should also be passed after a reasonable period of time.

Don't oppose without any reason, or without any rationale or without any idea whatsoever as to how long you want to keep going.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is time that the Canadian people had the right to take a very clear look at this House, and vote through their representatives. I suggest that that vote take place immediately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really deplorable and disappointing that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), after four days of debate, is doing the "dirty work" the Prime Minister has asked him to do, in other words, gagging the Opposition and presenting a motion of closure.
Mr. Speaker, after four days, this debate has only just started. The Government has not told us why it is in such a hurry to adopt a Bill that will not become effective until January 1.
The Government has not answered our questions. Why did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare not transfer the $15 million they are going to squeeze out of families with children in 1985-86 and the $40 million in 1986-87 to the child tax credit, by increasing the child tax credit and raising the cut-off point for families with modest and low incomes? Mr. Speaker, the Government has failed to answer that question. Why is it trying to gloss over the cuts in family allowance increases starting in 1986, when everybody knows that family allowance payments benefit poor families and families on modest and low incomes, since these payments are taxable? Nor has the Minister of National Health and Welfare told us why he is going to wait until 1987 to reduce the Child Tax Exemption, a measure that benefits those with higher incomes.
If we refer to the Blue Book signed by the previous speaker, Mr. Epp-I think it was Mr. Epp-and if we look at the table on page 17 under Child Tax Exemption, we see that families whose incomes are less than $10,000 receive no money at all under the Child Tax Exemption; families whose incomes are less than $20,000 receive a tax exemption of $203; but families with an income of $80,000 receive $363.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has failed to answer the question. It does not want this matter to be discussed. I can see why the Prime Minister is ashamed of his Bill. I can see why the Prime Minister wants to rush through the House a piece of legislation that is going to hurt families with modest and low incomes.
Mr. Speaker, on the weekend I met a number of mothers, and I think many Hon. Members will remember what these
September 24, 1985

mothers told me and what my mother used to say. Children used to ask their parents, and many Members will remember such moments, for $5 or $10 to buy school supplies, or a boy might want to buy a hockey stick or a pair of skates and a girl a pair of boots, and their mothers would say: Wait until the middle of the month when I get my family allowance cheque. Even today, Mr. Speaker, I meet families in the riding of Rosemont, a Conservative riding, in the riding of Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, also a Conservative riding, in the riding of Gamelin which is also a Conservative riding ... Even today, mothers tell us it is often very humiliating when they have to ask the teacher whether they can put off paying for some school activity for a week or two, until the family allowance cheque arrives.
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why the Prime Minister, who was not brought up in a rich family ... I can understand people who were raised in a rich family, where the family allowance cheque was not important. However, for the vast majority of families in Quebec, the family allowance cheque was often the only budget that the mothers administered, because the father kept all the money. Mr. Speaker, very often . . . Some Hon. Members will remember, for instance those from Quebec, that when they were little, they got a pair of winter boots because their mother could count on her family allowance cheque. Very often, girls were able to take part in activities like the majorettes as soon as their mothers got their family allowance cheques, Mr. Speaker. And they used to have large families in Quebec, and some of those families had food on the table thanks to their family allowance cheque!
I suppose the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers) is going to say: $4 a month is peanuts. Mr. Speaker, when families do not have enough money to start with, it is not peanuts. How can anyone understand why the Government wants to squeeze $55 million out of families with low incomes? The Government could have done what all the agencies recommended, and that was to reduce the tax exemption which benefits the rich and increase the tax credit as much as possible, and thus give families on modest and low incomes a bit more. How are people going to believe that the Government had no trouble finding $1.2 billion to help companies and individuals with bank deposits of over $60,000? These people knew the risks they were taking, Mr. Speaker. Why are all those other taxpayers, all those families going to have to pay for the mistakes made by this Government?
Mr. Speaker, I think it is unconscionable that after only four days of debate, the Government should decide to use closure. I can assure the Government that although it may be able to manipulate the proceedings and try to gag the Opposition here in the House, and I can also assure the Minister of social injustice of Canada that he will not be able to gag the Opposition in the streets. There will be a meeting tomorrow in Montreal. Tomorrow, Quebec families are going to start organizing in all ridings, and the Prime Minister will not be
Time Allocation
able to manipulate and gag these people. The debate will shift to the streets, to all kitchens and to the offices of Members, and the social injustice minister will always have in mind the shamelessness he displayed this morning, he who under normal circumstances, like all previous Ministers of National Health and Welfare, Liberals and Tories alike, ought to stand up in the House to defend the interests of poor families and elderly Canadians. For the first time in Canada's history a Minister of National Health and Welfare acts as a hatchet man against families.
Mr. Speaker, the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans had the courage to resign. Considering his pitiful performance in the debate on deindexation of old age security pensions and his failure to speak up against taxes on prescription drugs and additional levies on families with children, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have the courage to tender his resignation and ask for another portfolio. Mrs. Begin would have never put up with that, she would have resigned rather than do the dirty work of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The social injustice minister can be satisfied with himself, his $40,000 and his driver. He has it made and could not care less about others, but one of these days he will have to face up to the music when all those families come up here to challenge him.
Mr. Speaker, when we recall the Government promises we understand why the word of the Prime Minister does not mean much any more. The Government did make a commitment not to reduce the deficit at the expense of families, but after listening to the Minister of National Health and Welfare we have to ask what his word is worth today. Nothing. Before consulting with the various interest groups, the Minister of National Health and Welfare rose before the parliamentary committee to ask: Would the interest groups prefer that all funds be redistributed in the form of tax credits? Yes, they said. So he did exactly the opposite.
I see that my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, so I want to tell Hon. Members that for now this may be the end of the debate in the House, but I can assure them that I will take to the streets and strongly denounce both the social injustice minister and the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in this debate. It is my first chance to speak but, unfortunately, in so doing, I am not speaking on the issue itself because the Government has now introduced a time allocation motion. This is a motion which is known to most of the world as a closure motion.
It is interesting to note that in the opening of his speech the Minister mentioned that the former Liberal Government used this measure often in its term of office. That is quite true. It is also true that we New Democrats have often not spoken against the principle of time allocation because we agree that

September 24, 1985
Time Allocation
there must be some mechanism to ensure that there is orderly debate and some conclusion to debate in the House of Commons.
However, with regard to the particular issue before us, we are talking about a fundamental change in the universality of social programs in the country. The Government has slid over that point in debate. The Minister, in his long quotations from various newspapers, mentioned editorials from various parts of the country which spoke out in support of him. He did not mention those editorials which point out that the Government is, indeed, moving away from universality in this important area.
The attack on family allowances is just the beginning of the crack in the dam which we have in place to defend social programs in Canada. In his speech, the Minister spoke about the fact that we approved the Budget. With 211 Tory Members in the House of Commons we have to approve everything which is put forward. Let me remind the Minister that even though the House approved the Budget, the Government backed down with respect to the deindexing of old age pensions.
We have a right-an obligation-to stand up in the House of Commons to debate Bills and the philosophy behind them. We have a right to ensure that the public has an opportunity to know what is really in the legislation which the Government is presenting.
In defending his legislation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said that the money will be going from those who have a lot of it-the hypothetical banker in this nation-to peole who need it the most. That is the myth out there which is the foundation of the editorials from which the Minister has quoted. I would like to quote from another editorial. It is one which takes the opposite side. It is an editorial which appeared in yesterday's Winnipeg Free Press. I am sure the Minister is aware of it. This is an article written by Leonard Shifrin. First, it points out that the Government is again breaking another promise. The headline reads: "The Tories broke their word". The article points out that the Minister himself said that the Government would not be taking money from the old age pension, family allowances, et cetera, to reduce the deficit. The article further points out that in the long run, after a three-year period, it will not just be the middle-income earners, those with a fairly reasonable salary or those who are rich in Canada who will be losing the benefit of a fully indexed family allowance. It will be all Canadians who receive the family allowance, including those at the lowest level of the Canadian income scale. And the Government also plans to deindex the child tax credit which it is so fond of saying is the recipient of this money is going to be saved through the reduction to the full indexation of family allowances.
What the Government is doing is what we have always said is the dangerous thing about the move away from universality. It is a two-step operation. First, it reduces the dependency of
middle-income earners on the family allowance by taking away the protection of full indexation. In other words, over a period of time the real money which the average woman will receive from the family allowance-and let's make no mistake about it, that money in most cases goes to the woman and is spent by her for the necessities of the family-will be worth less and less to that family. The reduction by 3 per cent a year of the real value of the family allowances means that it will provide for less and less of the basic necessities for food, clothing and other items for the children of that family. That is the first step.
The second step is to deindex the child tax credit, the money which goes to the poorest families in this land. We see that as dangerous, Mr. Speaker, because the Government will take away broad public support for family allowances by making it worth less to a large percentage of the population. After it has done that, three years down the road, it will take the protection from those who need it the most. That is something of which the public is not aware and that is why we need a full debate.
My colleague from the Liberal Party mentioned that we have had only four days' debate on this issue. That is not very much. This is an issue which is fundamentally changing the way we deal with universal programs in this country.
The Government failed in its first attack. It failed to deindex the old age pensions. The new frontal assault now is to attack family allowances. That is a dangerous precedent and it is very important that the public be aware of exactly what the Government is doing.
It is also just as important, Mr. Speaker, that we have a chance to hear from that same public. As the public becomes more and more aware of what the Government is doing, as it realizes this is not just a short-term cut-back to reduce the deficit, as it becomes aware that this is not an attempt to take money away from those who are rich to give to those who are poor, as the public becomes more and more aware of what is really happening, there will be more and more groups who will tell this Government not to deindex family allowances.
That is what happened in the pension debate. It became a national issue. It took some time to get it going but after one month of debate, after one month of petitions, and after various groups came to the House of Commons saying that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had broken his word, the message got through to the Government.
It is now one week since the debate started in this House on the deindexation of family allowances and the Government wants to take this legislation away from the House of Commons. We have televised debates and the people who are out there can find out what is really in the legislation and will have a chance to respond to their Members of Parliament and the Minister responsible for this legislation. They will have a chance to tell the Prime Minister that he has broken faith once more with the population of this country. But the Government wants to shuffle the legislation into some committee room. That goes against the whole intent of televising the debates of the House of Commons.
September 24, 1985

We want the public to know what is going on. We want the public to know not only what is going on but to come back to us and tell us that they want to protect family allowances, that they want to protect the universality of Government programs.
We built a social net in this country, and I give full credit to all three political Parties for building that social net over many, many years. Now we have a Government dedicated, in a sneaky, two-step fashion, to breaking down that social net.
I think it is very important that we not be limited, as we are today, to a two-hour debate. Members from all Parties should stand up for the right of the public to know what is really going on in this legislation. They should stand up and tell the people of Canada that this is not just something which will deindex family allowances with the money going to the poor. They should explain what is really happening three years down the road when that money is going to be taken away not only from the rich, from the bank president the Prime Minister is so fond of referring to, but from the very people who need it most.
There is a public clamour for this Government to stop deindexation of family allowances. Some of the groups who have come out in support of full indexation of family allowances include the National Anti-Poverty Organization and the National Advisory Committee on the Status of Women. I met with 15 different groups in Nova Scotia two weeks ago and not one of them wanted to see this Government move ahead on this proposal. I am asking this Government and Members of Parliament to let the public participate in this debate, not in a closed hearing room but in this House of Commons itself, so we have a chance to make sure people know and approve of what this Government is doing, because they do not.

We want that legislation passed so that we enhance the income of low-income families and reduce the income of the higher income families. That is exactly what you are against.
I believe that the Government should have its bad legislation. That is what Churchill said. The question of whether it is bad legislation or not remains for the court of public opinion.
I suggest that the Opposition has failed miserably to mount any public opinion against this Bill. They know that, and they know it well. I believe very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that we should pick our spots when we bring in closure. We should have a full debate. seat to be able to hear that kind of an intervention. 1 hope that the people in his hometown will take the opportunity to listen to what he said. If they do, they will realize that the intent of this Government measure is a massive tax grab from middle income Canadians.
I would like to refer to a point made by my colleague from Montreal. It comes as no surprise to us on this side of the House that the Government has chosen to introduce time allocation in order to end the debate with respect to Bill C-70 on the floor of the House of Commons. The Government does not want to have the debate widened, as we do, in order to ensure that Canadians fully understand more than just the import of deindexation of familly allowances.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) quite properly read into the record from an editorial in last Friday's edition of The Toronto Star. However, he read selectively from it. The last paragraph of that editorial is the telling one. It indicates that Opposition MPs are misdirecting their fire by concentrating simply on he deindexation of the baby bonus, however popular a cause that may be with middle class voters. They should, instead, the mounting be barricades for the kind of meaningful reform of the tax and transfer payment system that would lead Canada to a better system of social security for its neediest citizens. That is what we have been attempting to do in this debate rather than simply focussing, as the Government wants us to, on its plan to deindex familly allowances.
I am looking forward to the debate that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will introduce on the floor of the House of Commons when the Government brings forward the omnibus tax Bill to deal with those other measures in the Budget which will impact on low and middle income Canadians in a manner in which the Government does not want average Canadian citizens to find out about.
When considering the Government's proposals we must include the plan to deindex personal exemptions. As a result of those two measures, at the end of 1990 a family of four living on $15,000 a year will pay an additional $1,700 in income taxes and a family of four living on $35,000 a year will pay an additional $3,600 in taxes, but a family of four living on $80,000 a year will only pay $1,125 more in taxes. In other words, the import of the over-all tax change is to make the rich richer and the poor poorer. That is what is at the heart of this debate.
The Government wanted Canadians to focus on its plan to deindex family allowances because it knows it can get away with this measure. The Government wants us to focus on what it is doing in the left pocket while it is taking thousands of dollars of income out of the right pocket. The net effect on Canadians will be that in four years the disposable income of the poorest of the poor in our society will be four per cent less, while the rich in our society will have an additional .6 per cent of disposable income.
September 24, 1985

I am not surprised by the fact that the Government has introduced time allocation, but 1 am surprised that it chose the Minister of National Health and Welfare to introduce it. The Minister of National Health and Welfare should have ensured that if time allocation had to be introduced, it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who introduced it. I know the quality of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and 1 am sure that he must have fought extremely hard around the Cabinet table, but lost the battle. I find it difficult to believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare could defend budgetary measures that will put the burden of deficit reduction on the backs of low and middle income Canadians rather than advocating, as he should, the overhaul of the tax system to introduce a minimum tax for the rich and to ensure that the transfer does not make the rich richer and the poor poorer. That is what middle and low income Canadians expect from the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The previous Minister of National Health and Welfare, Monique Begin, made a name as a defender of the interests of poor and middle income families in our society. She fought well at the Cabinet table to ensure that the interests of her constituents were well represented. They certainly have not been in this debate.
The Minister indicated that, rather than simply obstructing every piece of legislation, the Opposition should bring forward proposals to improve the system. In the intervention that I made on September 16 1 indicated the proposals and principles on which the Liberal Party will stand with respect to an overhaul of the social security system in the country. I indicated that we have certain premises with which we began. One of the premises is that amongst the OECD countries Canada ranks in the bottom third in terms of the percentage of GNP that goes to our social security system. That is a fact.

would hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would exercise his responsibility and indicate his displeasure at the direction which the Minister of Finance took on May 23.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commenting on some of the things said by previous speakers. I was interested in the benefit of the doubt which the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) gave to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). he hypothesized that the Minister had fought hard at the Cabinet table but had lost in the battle for family allowances. I hold no such theory. As far as 1 am concerned, I think the Minister is captive to the total economic philosophy of the Government. I do not think he fought very hard at the Cabinet table to prevent the partial deindexation of family allowances. I do not give him that benefit of the doubt. I have seen how the Minister of National Health and Welfare fights at the Cabinet table for other things, particularly for his own province, and he has been a miserable failure at that. If he fought at all to prevent the deindexation of family allowances, his record is equally miserable in that regard. I doubt whether he actually fought.
I was disappointed by the speech of the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) who said that he had been waiting to make such a speech for six years. Instead of making a reasoned defence of the need for the Government to pass its legislation-and indeed such a reasoned defence can be made-it turned out to be a political tirade totally captive to the present context. I was disappointed because I thought we might actually receive some erudite parliamentary advice from the Hon. Member.
In respect of the reason for closure, we have not debated the Bill at great length. The real reason is a political one, that the Government is afraid public opinion may be mobilized. Some people have argued that four months have gone by since the original suggestion was made. We have to remember that the political agenda is often crowded, as it has been since the time the proposal was first made. If the Government was confident that its measure had the support of the Canadian public, I think it would have been much more relaxed about allowing the debate to continue in the House for a decent period of time.
Before the summer recess the House was preoccupied and seized with the question of the deindexation of pensions, and there have been many items on the agenda since our return. One of the functions of delay in the parliamentary system is that it gives people time to catch on to what the Government is up to. I am unhappy, although I understand it as a political tactic, that the Government has decided to try to prevent that from happening. However, let us be clear about why this is being done.
Unfortunately the Minister of National Health and Welfare tried to make light of the position of the Opposition on family allowances. What he did not do or what he could have done-

September 24, 1985
Time Allocation
and, in doing so, I think he could have enhanced his own image-was recognize that what we have here is a debate about fundamentals in so far as social policy is concerned. He could have dwelled on matters of principle, but he did not do that because the Conservative approach to the whole question of family allowances and other social policy changes has been completely devoid of principle. It is no accident that the Minister did not try to get into that higher level of debate which was available to him.
We see a total lack of principle on the part of the Government. The real principle in the backs of the minds of many Progressive Conservative Members, whether they be in Cabinet or on the back-benches, is that they do not like universal social programs. I would much rather that they had the guts to say it and to initiate a debate on universality. This is what they should be trying to do instead of trying to get rid of universality by the back door and not having the commitment to their own fundamental view of social policy. We are not afraid to travel around the country saying that we stand by universal social programs even when some people in the social policy area have questions about universality. We are willing to take that heat, but the Conservative Party is not willing to take the heat about its own real position. Its Members are not able to do that or are unwilling to do that.
There was a second position which they could have adopted on principle, which they did not do. They could have stuck by their contention that whatever reforms they made, the money saved through such reforms would have been passed on to those people who needed it the most. That was the position of principle which they took in the paper released by the Minister of National Health and Welfare back in January, I believe it was, but they abandoned that principle. They did not have the guts to stick by it. Now we find that the money which is to be saved from the deindexation of family allowances will eventually find its way into the cause of deficit reduction rather than into the pockets and budgets of families who need it most. By doing this, the Government made a serious political error, if I may give it some unsolicited advice. Had its Members stuck by the second principle, they could have divided their critics. Had they stuck by that principle, groups which are now forming a coalition against the deindexation of family allowances would have been divided over the issue because some of them would have said that if the money was actually going to those who needed it most, they would support the Government. Certain groups have taken that position over the years, but the Conservatives did not have the guts to stick by that principle. Now we see a coalition of people from various groups that have held various views about the benefits of universality over the years coming together to say that this is bad social policy in every respect because it erodes universality without adopting the most beneficial aspects of selectivity. Also they say that it is a retreat on promises made by the Government in January in respect of where money saved would go and, before that, the promises made by its Members during the election campaign about whether family allowances would be hit at all.
I recall that the Progressive Conservative candidate who was my opponent in the last election had conniptions when I distributed a pamphlet indicating that the Conservatives would tamper with family allowances. He said that that was a lie, that I was a most irresponsible person and that the Progressive Conservative Party had no intention of doing anything with family allowances. He asked how I could be so dishonest and make those kinds of allegations. I said the same about pensions. Of course many members of the New Democratic Party did, because we know the real social policy agenda of the Progressive Conservative Party. Unfortunately the Conservatives are unwilling to come forward to say so, so that we can have a real debate about the fundamentals of social policy. 1 think that would be instructive for all of us; we could find out where people really are in respect of these issues.
It is not only questions of social policy, it is also the question of who is pro-family, if anyone is completely. There has been much rhetoric about who is pro-family and who is anti-family. However, the deindexation of family allowances and the erosion of universality over time will not be an attack only upon families. It is an attack on communities and on the sense of what it means to be a community.
One of the reasons we are in favour of universal social programs is that we believe a community has the right to say that it regards certain matters as important. In this case it is the family. It might be education or retirement for the elderly. We say that these things are provided to people because we believe that that is what it means to be part of a community. We believe that they ought to be allocated to people on the basis of the fact that they are part of the community, not because they are at one end or the other of the income scale, nor because we hold to a view of society which sees us as isolated individuals.
We have a notion of what it means to be a community. That is also at stake here, in terms of the philosophical debate wich we ought to be having. We will not have the time to do that. In fact, we will not have as much time as we need because the Government has chosen to move a closure motion. It goes against everything its Members said in Opposition. When it comes down to it, they did not mean it in any event. It is too bad that we will not have time for the debate we ought to be having.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in the debate on the motion moved by my Hon. colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). I believe that Bill C-70 should immediately be referred to the legislative committee which is empowered to make an in-depth study of its provisions. I want to express my support for this Bill. Being myself a mother who received family allowances for her four children, I understand the crucial importance of this debate for all recipients of family allowances, especially women.
September 24, 1985

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my intervention is twofold. First, I shall emphasize the universal nature of family allowances and the progressiveness of the federal child benefit system. Second, I shall outline the main reasons which motivated our Government to index family allowances yearly to the consumer price index over 3 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is my duty to reassure the Canadian people that the principle of universality of the family allowances system will be maintained. This system, after being established in 1945, soon became popular with Canadian society as a whole. Through this system, the Governments recognize the invaluable contributions made to society by parents who are raising tomorrow's citizens. In 1985, some 3.6 million Canadian families will receive $2.45 billion under the family allowances system. These 3.6 million Canadian families can be assured that the Conservative Government has no intention of jeopardizing the universality of this system. In spite of the recommendation by the Commission on the Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada to the effect that family allowances and other Federal transfers should be replaced by a universal income security system, my colleague, the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare, clearly stated that the Government had preferred to maintain the principle of universality and indexation. I find it very regrettable that our friends opposite would remain silent about the fact that the universality of this program is being maintained. Throughout this debate, they have tried to scare the Canadian people, but it should be emphasized that the Government of which I am a member is in no way contesting the universality of family allowances.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this Bill must be viewed as only one component in the federal child benefit package. Consequently, it must not be considered in isolation, but should instead be analyzed in conjunction with the other two components, namely the child tax credit and the tax exemption for dependent children.
In a spirit of social justice, our Government has shown its desire to reinforce the progressive nature of the programs designed to provide financial assistance to people with children. Is it not more equitable, Mr. Speaker, to pay higher benefits to the poorer recipients and the lower benefits to the wealthiest? A report of the National Welfare Council entitled The Reform of Child Benefits tabled in March 1985 concluded that "the benefits received by a family from the child benefit system have no logical or equitable relation with its financial needs". According to this same report, "the Canadian child benefit system is inconsistent not because it provides benefits to high income families, but rather because their benefits are too high. It is a problem of equity".
Improving the progressiveness of family allowances is therefore a basic objective to which our Government has committed itself. A number or organizations dedicated to the defence of the disadvantaged have for many years requested from the

speechtext:
This Bill, if it passes, will hurt 3.6 million Canadian families by reducing the purchasing power of the family allowance. No wonder the Conservatives want to choke off debate on this Bill after only five days. The Conservatives hope this Bill will slip through this House before Canadians, especially middle and lower income Canadians, fully realize what harm the Conservatives want to do to them.
The Conservatives now say that there has been enough debate on this whole issue of deindexing the family allowance. The last speaker, in particular, cast doubt upon the commitment of the Conservatives even to the most elementary of social programs. Yet back in 1980, the Conservatives had a massive ad campaign opposing any suggestion of deindexing. That ad said in part that deindexing "is a form of taxation that will have staggering consequences for every Canadian taxpayer, especially the low income earner". It said that "deindexing is a scheme to guarantee that you will pay higher federal income taxes year after year". If that was true in 1980 with respect to income tax, it is true today, not just for income tax but for family allowance.
Yet the Conservatives today are trying to cut off debate on a measure aimed at slipping through a cruel blow to a key part
September 24, 1985

of our whole fabric of programs to support families and all Canadians. No wonder the Conservatives want to rush through an amendment to the Family Allowance Act which is something as I have said, that severely weakens and undermines the objectives of one of the fundamental elements of our national social security framework.
The Bill which this motion wants to bring to a vote reduces the indexing of family allowances and therefore its purchasing power. This not only contradicts promises made by the Conservative Party in the last election campaign, it absolutely contradicts the assurances of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who stated in this House last December 21, and I quote from Hansard at page 1444:
Mr. Speaker, 1 can confirm that the regular indexing of the Old Age Security, Guaranteed Income Suplement, and family allowance will be increased as of January 1, 1985, and the Canada Pension Plan will also be increased 4.4 per cent-
The question asked of the Minister at that time did not include any reference to the family allowance system which is under attack today. However, the Minister went out of his way to include the family allowance in his commitment to increase regular indexing for 1985. The indexed family allowance benefits will increase by 4.4 per cent in 1985 but will be 1.4 per cent, more or less, in 1986, because of this cruel and heartless Bill.
The Family Allowance Bill of 1973 was introduced by the Liberal Government of the day and was approved by this House with the support of all Parties. That Bill had as its objective the strengthening of an income supplement program for Canadian families which was created by a Liberal Government almost 30 years before. This law was passed with the full recognition that income from employment does not request family size, that family bread winners working at or near the minimum, part-time or full-time, often do not have sufficient earnings to support more than one or two dependent children.
The Family Allowance Act also embodies a recognition that the family bread winner may only be able to obtain work on a seasonal or intermittent basis. Parliamentarians realized that these families constantly struggle to keep off the welfare roles because of their pride in their ability to make their own way. Indexing was and is very much part of the program to preserve the purchasing power of the family allowance, a vital instrument, therefore, of social justice.
It is not only this particular Tory Bill under debate today which violates the objectives of the Family Allowance Act and our entire social security framework. This legislation is just one part of a total package of Conservative Government Budget measures which runs against the grain of every positive step taken by successive federal Governments-yes, Liberal Governments-to help lower and middle income Canadian families to improve their economic and social standing in the society of our country.
Further, the May Budget of the Conservatives is not just fundamentally flawed in its brutalizing collision with the values which have shaped our national social policy tradition and consensus, it strikes particularly at lower and middle
Time Allocation
income Canadians at a time when we are still in a period of recovery from a severe world-wide recession. Lower and middle income Canadians have borne the brunt of general economic difficulty.
The May Budget of this Conservative Government will drive an expanding wedge through an already widening gap between rich and middle-income and poor families. At a time when federal Government anti-poverty efforts should be renewed and reinforced, at a time when federal government efforts to assist families should be strenghened, this Tory Government has chosen to redistribute income from lower and middle-income Canadians to rich Canadians.
This Government's first priority is an impersonal passion for the bottom line. It intends to apply what it calls savings, actually money taken from the pockets of middle and lower-income Canadians in the billions of dollars through cuts in social programs, to reducing the deficit.
First it tried to do that with the old age pension and the outrage of Canadians generally forced it back. But it still wants to do this to the family allowance program, the subject of the Bill which this motion will bring to a vote. It intends to do the same thing to the indexing of the personal income tax. The so-called savings are to be applied to a reduction of the deficit and the Government intends to do this as a priority in total disregard of its own promise, stated for example by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on December 14 of last year, that none of the money saved by reducing social benefit payments would be used to reduce the deficit. So much for credibility. So much for accuracy. So much for a commitment to social values by this cruel and heartless Conservative Government.
Even this cynical passion for deficit reduction fails to completely explain Tory Government motives which result in the unfairness of the Budget of which this Bill is just one part. While the Government has been forced to withdraw its measure to deindex the OAS, it continues to try to put into effect tax policy which would provide a small group of individuals who receive handsome profits from capital gains with unconditional exemptions which will cause lost tax revenues estimated at $1.2 billion in 1990 alone.
The Budget proposes a swath of changes to child benefits which, according to the superficial arguments of the Government, appear to provide an advantage for low-income families. But on closer examination we find this Budget will bring about a partial deindexing at the 3 per cent threshold after 1989; that the cut-off point for the planned child tax credit reduction will be lowered from $26,330 to $23,000 in 1986; and that the child tax exemption will be reduced from $710 per child to $560 in 1987, $470 in 1988, and to the level of the family allowance in 1989. Every Canadian family will lose necessary benefits as a result of the impact of the Conservative Budget. But even the poorest of the poor will lose benefits after 1990 because of the deindexation of the child tax credit along with the deindexation of the family allowance which the Conserva-

September 24, 1985
Time Allocation
tives are trying to force through this House today against the interests of Canadian families and children. All families will get less, even the poorest will get less, because of this Conservative measure.
If we consider the cumulative impact of the budget measures to change the child tax credit and the current tax exemptions for dependant children, and the indexation of income tax, then we find working parents who together earn $15,000 annually and have to feed, clothe and provide a home for only two children, will lose $1,844. The husband and wife who earn a combined annual income of $35,000 will lose $3,452.
There is no reasonable and objective standard of evaluation of the Conservative Budget, of which this Bill is just one harmful part, which can avoid yielding the conclusion of unfairness and injustice. The consistent and undeniable theme throughout is a redistribution of disposable income away from lower and middle-income taxpayers to upper-income taxpayers. Over the next five years those earning $15,000 a year will have to absorb a 36 per cent tax increase, those earning $30,000 an 11 per cent tax increase, those earning $100,000 only a 4 per cent tax increase, and those few taxpayers, great friends of the Tories obviously, earning $200,000 a year will only have to pay 2 per cent more in taxes. That is Tory fairness. That is Tory social justice.
To conclude, in December of last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appeared to base the entire argument for his Government's unsuccessful attack on the universality of certain social programs on the justice he saw contained in his tirelessly repeated and meaningless anecdote of how bank presidents should not be receiving social programs benefit payments which they do not need or want. He tried to give Canadians the impression that his Government would redirect and enrich social program benefits to Canadians most in need. Well, the Canadian people were not taken in when it came to the OAS and in spite of Conservative efforts to choke off debate on this Bill they will not be taken in by its measures.
Certainly the imbalance, unfairness and injustice of the Budget in general and this measure in particular have only been made more patently obvious by the Government's total mismanagement of its reponsibility in the $1 billion fiasco involving the Canadian Commercial and Northland Banks. While the Conservative Government places an onerous burden of taxation on lower and middle-income Canadians, it is ready to spend more than $1 billion of the taxpayers' money to make up for its mishandling of the CCB affair. The Government should withdraw its Budget and keep its promises to lower and middle-income Canadians. This Bill, as one step to withdrawing this Budget, should be defeated; the first step is to defeat this motion aimed at unfairly choking off debate on this important measure.

Mr. Speaker, for more than five months a number of employees of the Kresge department store chain in Thunder Bay have been on strike in an attempt to win a first contract and ensure for themselves a reasonable degree of recognition and remuneration for their work. Ninety-four per cent of these employees are women and,
September 24, 1985

as is the case far too often when the majority of employees are women, the management of this company is trying to ignore them. These employees receive an average wage of only $4.51 per hour, which is far below the poverty line for a single mother. An employee with 30 years of service with the company will receive a whopping pension of less than $90 per month.
These workers have every right to demand fair compensation for their work, and the company has a social responsibility to deal with them fairly and to accept their right to form a union to speak with a collective voice. If the company refuses to live up to its responsibilities, then it is up to society to impose sanctions. The workers are asking the consumers of Canada to boycott this department store chain, and the other chains, K-Mart, Jupiter, and Big Top which have the same owners.
This boycott has been offered support from the CLC, the OFL, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Thunder Bay, and the United Food and Commercial Workers. I hope it will also be endorsed by all consumers of Canada who understand that fairness and a decent standard of living are the right of all workers in this country. I ask that they join with me and my colleagues and say: "I can't shop at Kresge's any more!"

Mr. Speaker, I would again like to bring to the attention of the House the matter of the elimination of pass privileges by CP Rail for CP Rail pensioners. When the issue first came to light last summer CP Rail indicated that it was a decison arrived at during union-management negotiations. CP Rail has now indicated that passes for pensioners and employees were a privilege and not a right, and that they have been replaced by a comprehensive health package at no cost to the pensioners. Pensioners, as well as all residents of my constituency, are already fully covered by our provincial health plan.
The letter of September 16, 1985, from the President of CP Rail addressed to all CP Rail retirees falls far short of providing an adequate explanation regarding the elimination of these pass privileges.
There was a clearly documented agreement between union and management, dating back to 1936, that employees of the CPR, and pensioners who retired in good standing, were entitled to pass privileges for life.
The CPR received land grants and mineral rights as well as many financial advantages during the planning and construction stage. In view of this, Mr. Speaker, I call on CP Rail to accept its corporate responsibilities and restore pass privileges to all pensioners.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT WITHDRAW BILL C-70
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT WITHDRAW BILL C-70
speechtext:
Last weekend, Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity to meet with several mothers and a good many people responsible for family organizations, and they all wanted to know what the word of the Government is worth. They reminded me that the consultation paper tabled by the Government last January concerning child benefits contains a sentence which goes like this: "The commitment of the Government is that no savings resulting from program changes should be transferred to deficit reduction". A few months later, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled a Budget document stating that net federal expenditures will be reduced by $15 million in 1985-86 and by $40 million in 1986-87. All this money, $55 million, will come from cut backs in income support programs for families with children.
Those people are also wondering why the Government did not implement the unanimous recommendations made by various groups whereby the child tax credit exemption should be reduced because it benefits wealthier people. According to the document, a well-to-do- person with an income of $80,000 will get $363 more whereas a man with a $10,000 income does not get anything. Those people would just like to know why the Prime Minister and his Conservative Government do not honour their words and commitments and withdraw Bill C-70.

OPPOSITION TO SOVIET AUTHORITIES PROVIDING EVIDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Deschenes Commission of Inquiry heard arguments regarding the possibility of the Commission travelling to the Soviet Union to gather evidence. Taking into consideration the abominable record of human rights violations by the U.S.S.R., does the Commission really expect to find evidence that has not been tampered with and tainted?
Members of Parliament asked to appear before the Commission to address this very question of Soviet evidence and the merits of such a proposed trip. They were denied the opportunity to voice their views and those of their constituents. How can the Commission naively believe that Soviet authorities have justice in mind when they themselves committed atrocities during the war and continue to be the most repressive Government in modern times?
It is even more surprising, Mr. Speaker, to hear groups which so effectively discredited the Soviet judicial system, especially with regard to trials against Soviet citizens, now argue that the Commission would be shirking its responsibility if it did not go to the U.S.S.R. The Commission would be in a

jurisdiction where the presumption of innocence and judicial independence are not the rule of law. If such evidence is accepted by the commission established by the Government of Canada, it will, in effect, be approving and accepting the present legal system of the U.S.S.R., a system that is corrupt. Canadians will never give approval to such abrogation of fundamental freedoms.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-DEMAND FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
SOUTH AFRICA-DEMAND FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in response to questions asked about South African controlled mining companies operating in Canada are a result of the Government's lack of a definite policy toward South Africa. Canadians in one-industry towns such as Flin Flon and Snow Lake in Manitoba feel extremely nervous as a result of the Minister's spontaneous remarks. Fear has been created in these communities, yet the Government has no clear policy.
Personally, I continue to support strong sanctions that will affect the South African Government's oppressive policy of apartheid. However, there must be a clear statement of this Government's policy. Without that we suffer from vague remarks that create unnecessary fears. Let us hope that this is the last example of another Minister, another foot, and another mouth.

subtopic: NEED TO BUILD FRIGATES AT LAUZON, QUE.
NEED TO BUILD FRIGATES AT LAUZON, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has already been brought to the attention of this House that Versatile-Davie is going to build the equivalent of one and a half frigates in Lauzon, thus creating jobs for 650 workers in this area for four years. This decision was made by the company's management after considering the following factors:
The alternative site had not been used for shipbuilding since 1968;
Shipbuilding in modular phases had already been tried in Lauzon but never at the other site;
Human resources and equipment at Versatile-Davie were in a better position to accelerate the development of Canadian expertise and thus strengthen Canada's competitive position throughout the world.
The management of Versatile-Davie does not expect any interference from the Government in selecting the site because
it has already been said that this Government trusts the private sector to develop and enhance this country's economy.
The Government will neither obstruct nor interfere with the private sector's initiative, creativity, profitability and expansion. The development of Canadian expertise and our competitive position internationally make it imperative that the frigates be built in Lauzon.

Mr. Speaker, in a recent television interview the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) demeaned and insulted new Canadians by referring to an alleged syndrome that neither I nor any other new Canadian I have spoken to has ever observed. Specifically, the Prime Minister implied that immigrants tend to salute uniformed persons, something that I have never seen in this country.
One of the things that attracts immigrants from all countries to Canada is that it is a free country. That freedom is, of course, in no way threatened by the Prime Minister's rather feeble sense of humour. However, given the influence of his position, he should know better than to make any remark which would initiate or perpetuate negative stereotyping, however minor it may appear to him.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
According to our information, the Prime Minister's Office had been aware as early as July that Canada's two largest English language television networks were working on a story on the tainted tuna issue, as it is now referred to. Did the Prime Minister give his office instructions to be concerned, above all else, about the Prime Minister's image rather than the health and well-being of Canadians?

subtopic: ROLE OF PRIME MINISTER S OFFICE
speechtext:
What a surprising question from such a well-known and respected Member of this House!
Yesterday, I answered all questions fully and frankly. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member was not in the House. We have acted at all times with dispatch and in the interests of Canadian consumers.
My hon. friend mentioned the fact that one or two members of my staff were aware of the matter. It is true that Mr. MacAdam, a member of my staff, became aware of the existence of rumours around the first week of July. He got in touch with the Executive Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and received the assurance that there was no problem.
The second time was around the middle of July when Mr. Anderson, who works in my office, was visited by two staff members of the Minister concerned. He was given the assur-

Since the Minister was absent, Mr. Anderson was asked for advice on what to do if the issue was mentioned on the evening news. Mr. Anderson said: Take your most senior official at Fisheries and Oceans and make him fully available to the media, to answer any questions they might have. And that was it. I think my staff acted quickly, in the national interest, and I believe my hon. friend will agree that was the case.
